internship.title: Python Web Development Internship
internship.description: A serious, industry-oriented Python web development internship built around progressive engineering work rather than a renamed course. The intern begins with reproducible Python/Git and HTTP foundations, then works through Django architecture, relational data modeling, secure browser workflows, JSON APIs, automated testing, debugging, code review, performance, deployment readiness, and one substantial independent capstone. The program uses a coherent stack—Python 3.14.x, Django 6.1.1, Django REST framework, PostgreSQL, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, and pytest/pytest-django—so the intern learns how application code, data, security boundaries, tests, and operations fit together.
prerequisites: Basic Python: variables, functions, classes, exceptions, modules, file handling.
Basic SQL including SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, primary keys, and foreign keys.
Basic Git concepts are helpful but are reinforced.
objectives: Build and maintain a Python web application with Django.
Model relational data and use the Django ORM with PostgreSQL-oriented configuration.
Implement secure forms, sessions, authentication, authorization, and CSRF-protected state changes.
Design and implement a JSON API with Django REST framework.
Write automated tests and turn confirmed defects into regression coverage.
Review and improve query performance using measurement and query plans.
Prepare secure deployment configuration, static assets, logging, health checks, and release documentation.
Deliver and explain a complete end-to-end capstone.

modules.title: Python Web Engineering Foundations
modules.description: Establish a reproducible Python development environment and the HTTP/Git mental models that support professional web work.
objectives: Set up an isolated Python environment and verify interpreter/package-manager identity.
Trace an HTTP request and explain the responsibilities of browser, web server, framework, and database.
Use Git with safe repository hygiene and focused commits.
Diagnose interpreter, dependency, and import problems systematically.

lessons.title: Virtual environments and package isolation
lessons.description: Use Python virtual environments and a predictable dependency workflow.
learningObjectives: Create and activate a .venv on Unix-like systems and Windows.
Explain why isolation prevents dependency collisions.

notes.text: Why isolation matters

Python documentation describes virtual environments as isolated environments for project-specific interpreters and packages. Treat them as disposable: keep project code outside the environment and do not commit the environment directory.

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip --version

items: Keep .venv out of version control.
Use the interpreter that will actually run the application.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a project virtual environment?
options: To remove Python from the machine
quiz.answer: To isolate project dependencies
quiz.explanation: A virtual environment gives the project its own package context so unrelated applications do not share the same installed dependencies.

summary: An isolated environment reduces accidental dependency coupling.
Reproducibility starts with knowing exactly which interpreter and packages are active.

lessons.title: HTTP request and response lifecycle
lessons.description: Build a mental model for how a browser request reaches Python application code.
learningObjectives: Distinguish method, URL, headers, body, and status code.

notes.text: The web contract

An HTTP exchange has a request and a response. The application receives input, chooses a handler, performs work such as validation and database access, then produces a response with status, headers, and content.

items: Do not confuse authentication with routing.
A route identifies an application handler; it is not itself an authorization decision.

practicals.title: Create a reproducible Python workspace
practicals.description: Create and verify a local project environment.
steps: Activate it using the platform-specific activation command.
Create a .gitignore that excludes .venv, __pycache__, .env, and test caches.
practicals.output: The commands identify the active interpreter and pip, and the environment itself is excluded from Git.

quiz.question: Which layer in a Django application primarily maps a URL pattern to a view?
quiz.answer: URL configuration
quiz.explanation: Django URL configuration maps incoming paths to view callables.

summary: HTTP semantics guide both browser behavior and API design.
Status codes communicate the outcome of request processing.

lessons.title: Git workflow and repository hygiene
lessons.description: Use Git as an engineering tool for review, rollback, and reproducibility.
learningObjectives: Keep secrets and generated artifacts out of source control.

notes.text: A repository is part of the deliverable
A reviewer needs a coherent history, reproducible setup, and clear separation between source code and local state. Commit small changes that represent one intent.

git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initialize Python web project"
git switch -c feature/health-endpoint
Never commit real credentials, API keys, password files, or production secrets.

quiz.question: Why should a commit represent one coherent change?
quiz.answer: It improves review and rollback
quiz.explanation: A focused commit has a clear purpose, making the change easier to inspect, discuss, and revert.

summary: Focused commits make changes easier to review and revert.
Repository hygiene is part of professional engineering practice.

lessons.title: Debugging dependency and import failures
lessons.description: Develop a repeatable troubleshooting loop for local development failures.
learningObjectives: Confirm interpreter identity before changing code.
Inspect installed packages with python -m pip.
Use tracebacks to identify the first actionable failure.

notes.text: Debug from the environment inward
When an import fails, first establish which interpreter is executing the command, then inspect the environment that interpreter sees. Only after that should you modify application logic.

python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.version)"
python -m pip list

quiz.question: What is a good first check for ModuleNotFoundError?
options: Verify the package is installed in the active interpreter
quiz.answer: Verify the package is installed in the active interpreter
quiz.explanation: The active interpreter and its package environment determine module resolution.

summary: Environment diagnosis precedes application diagnosis.
Change one variable at a time and reproduce the smallest failure.

tasks.title: Build an environment diagnostic command
tasks.description: Create a one-command Python diagnostic for a new developer machine.
tasks.problemStatement: The team needs a script that reports the Python executable, Python version, and whether Django can be resolved by the active interpreter.
objectives: Print sys.executable and the Python version.
Use importlib.util.find_spec to check Django.
Return exit status 1 when Django is unavailable.
constraints: Do not hard-code an interpreter path.
Do not report success after a failed dependency check.
tasks.hint: Use sys.executable, sys.version, find_spec, and SystemExit.
tasks.solutionCode:
import importlib.util
import sys

def main():
    print(f"Python executable: {sys.executable}")
    print(f"Python version: {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    if importlib.util.find_spec("django") is None:
        print("Django: NOT FOUND")
        return 1
    print("Django: available")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
tasks.solutionExplanation: The script reports facts from the active runtime instead of assuming a fixed machine layout. It uses a non-zero exit code for missing Django so another tool could detect failure.

tasks.title: Create a safe Git baseline
tasks.description: Prepare a repository that another intern can clone without inheriting local state.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a .gitignore, README, initial commit, and feature branch for a Python web project.
objectives: Exclude .venv, .env, bytecode, caches, and local SQLite files.
Document environment setup at a high level.
Create a focused initial commit and branch.
constraints: Do not include real secrets in documentation.
Do not claim the repository contains files you did not create.
tasks.solutionCode:
# .gitignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.env
db.sqlite3
.pytest_cache/

# README excerpt
# Python Web Project

Create a .venv, activate it, install dependencies, and run the test suite.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The baseline separates source from local environment state and documents a reproducible development workflow.

modules.assessment: Review environment reproducibility, repository hygiene, and debugging method.

modules.title: Django Architecture and Server-Rendered Web Apps
modules.description: Build the first working Django application using project/app separation, routes, views, templates, forms, and environment-aware settings.
objectives: Create a Django project and application with clear boundaries.
Implement named routes, views, templates, and static assets.
Configure environment-driven secrets and deployment-sensitive settings.

lessons.title: Project and app structure
lessons.description: Understand Django project configuration versus domain applications.
learningObjectives: Identify settings, URL configuration, ASGI/WSGI entry points, and app modules.

notes.text: A Django project contains configuration for the overall site. A Django app groups a coherent domain capability such as tickets, billing, or inventory. This separation keeps URL wiring and configuration from swallowing domain logic.

django-admin startproject config .
python manage.py startapp tickets

quiz.question: Where should a Django domain model normally live?
quiz.answer: The app models module
quiz.explanation: Django models belong to application code and define the domain-to-database mapping.

summary: Use apps to represent domain capabilities.
Keep configuration centralized and domain logic inside the relevant app.

lessons.title: URL routing, views, and redirects
lessons.description: Implement routes using path converters, named URLs, and views.

items: Named URLs make redirects and template links resilient to path changes.
Use typed converters when the domain expects a specific value type.

quiz.question: What does the `<int:ticket_id>` converter do?
options: Converts the path segment to an integer
quiz.answer: Converts the path segment to an integer
quiz.explanation: Django parses the captured segment and passes an integer to the view.

summary: Routing maps external paths to internal handlers.
Named URLs reduce path duplication.

lessons.title: Templates, context, and static files
lessons.description: Render HTML with reusable templates and static assets.
learningObjectives: Load static assets with Django template tags.

notes.text: Templates are for presentation. Data preparation and business decisions belong in Python code; the template should render the prepared context.
Keep autoescaping enabled for normal user content. Do not bypass escaping casually.

quiz.question: What is a primary benefit of template inheritance?
quiz.answer: It centralizes reusable page structure
quiz.explanation: A base template can define shared layout while child templates fill blocks.

summary: Template inheritance keeps common layout in one place.
Static asset paths should be resolved through Django’s static-file system.

lessons.title: Settings and environment configuration
lessons.description: Keep secrets outside source control and make deployment-specific behavior explicit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish local DEBUG behavior from production settings.
Use Django deployment checks before release.

notes.text:
import os
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]
DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "false").lower() in {"1", "true"}
ALLOWED_HOSTS = [x.strip() for x in os.environ.get("DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS", "").split(",") if x.strip()]

items: Never commit a real production secret.
A passing deployment check is useful but is not a complete security assessment.

quiz.question: Why should SECRET_KEY not be committed?
options: It is sensitive configuration that should remain secret
quiz.answer: It is sensitive configuration that should remain secret
quiz.explanation: Django’s deployment guidance treats SECRET_KEY as sensitive and advises keeping it confidential.

summary: Configuration is part of application correctness.
Secrets belong in deployment configuration, not source code.

tasks.title: Implement a server-rendered ticket list
tasks.description: Build a read-only Django page using named routing, a view, a template, and a stylesheet.
tasks.problemStatement: Expose `/tickets/` and render two in-memory tickets with accessible links.
objectives: Create a named route.
Render context data with a loop and empty-state branch.
Use a static stylesheet.
constraints: Do not add a database dependency for this task.
Keep the sample data in Python.
tasks.hint: Use render(), path(), `{% for %}`, and `{% static %}.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task focuses on the request-to-template path before persistence is introduced.

tasks.title: Externalize deployment settings
tasks.description: Refactor hard-coded settings into environment variables and document the configuration contract.
tasks.problemStatement: A code review finds hard-coded debug and secret settings. Replace them with environment-driven configuration.
objectives: Read SECRET_KEY from an environment variable.
Parse a debug flag safely.
Parse comma-separated allowed hosts.
constraints: Do not commit usable secret values.
Do not use bool("false") as the boolean parser.
tasks.hint: Treat configuration strings as untrusted input and parse them deliberately.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The configuration is portable between environments while keeping real secrets out of source control.

modules.assessment: Review the application boundary between configuration, routing, and presentation.

modules.title: Relational Data Modeling and Django ORM
modules.description: Design the issue-tracker data model, use migrations and QuerySets, and reason about relationships, transactions, indexes, and database performance.
objectives: Model one-to-many and many-to-many relationships.
Create and inspect migrations.
Use filtering, ordering, pagination, relationship loading, and transactions.
Explain index trade-offs and the N+1 query problem.

lessons.title: Models, relationships, and constraints
lessons.description: Create a relational domain model with database-enforced invariants.
learningObjectives: Add unique constraints for domain rules.

notes.text: Application validation improves user experience, while database constraints protect invariants even when a write bypasses the intended form.

quiz.question: What is a unique database constraint for?
quiz.answer: Enforcing a uniqueness invariant
quiz.explanation: The database rejects inserts or updates that violate the unique constraint.

summary: Schema design is the foundation for safe and maintainable data access.
Constraints should express rules the database must always uphold.

lessons.title: Migrations and schema evolution
lessons.description: Use Django migrations as versioned schema changes.
learningObjectives: Explain why staged schema changes may be needed during deployment.

notes.text:
python manage.py makemigrations
python manage.py sqlmigrate tickets 0001
python manage.py migrate

items: Treat migrations as deployable artifacts.
Review destructive or large schema changes before production rollout.

quiz.question: Which command applies pending migrations?
quiz.answer: python manage.py migrate
quiz.explanation: `migrate` applies the migration graph to the configured database.

summary: Migrations connect model state to database evolution.
Schema compatibility can matter when old and new application versions overlap.

lessons.title: QuerySets, relationships, and pagination
lessons.description: Build efficient collection queries and prevent avoidable query explosions.
learningObjectives: Choose select_related or prefetch_related based on relationship cardinality.

notes.text:
tickets = (
    Ticket.objects
    .filter(status="open")
    .select_related("assignee")
    .prefetch_related("labels")
    .order_by("-updated_at", "-id")
)
QuerySets are lazy until evaluated, allowing composition. Performance problems commonly appear when related objects are accessed inside loops without appropriate loading.

quiz.question: Which optimization is designed for a foreign-key relation?
quiz.answer: select_related
quiz.explanation: select_related uses SQL joins for suitable single-valued relations such as foreign keys.

summary: Use measured query behavior to guide optimization.
select_related is suited to single-valued relations; prefetch_related is suited to related collections.

lessons.title: Transactions, indexes, and PostgreSQL
lessons.description: Use transactions when atomicity matters and add indexes based on measured access patterns.
learningObjectives: Explain why indexes improve some reads but add write/storage cost.
Use PostgreSQL EXPLAIN to investigate query plans.

notes.text:
from django.db import transaction

with transaction.atomic():
    ticket.status = "closed"
    ticket.save(update_fields=["status", "updated_at"])
    Comment.objects.create(ticket=ticket, author=actor, body="Closed")
Django recommends PostgreSQL for production while also supporting other relational databases. Index design should follow actual query patterns and measurements rather than guesswork.

quiz.question: What does transaction.atomic provide?
quiz.answer: An atomic database transaction boundary
quiz.explanation: Operations inside the block are committed or rolled back as a transaction according to Django transaction semantics.

summary: Transactions protect all-or-nothing business operations.
Query plans provide evidence for database performance decisions.

tasks.title: Build the core ticket schema
tasks.description: Implement Ticket, Comment, and Label models with relationships, timestamps, indexes, and a uniqueness constraint.
tasks.problemStatement: The issue tracker needs tickets owned by users, comments authored by users, and optional labels. Ticket titles must be unique per owner.
objectives: Implement the relationships.
Add status choices and timestamps.
Add a composite uniqueness constraint and useful indexes.
constraints: Use the built-in Django ORM.
Do not enforce uniqueness only in Python.
tasks.hint: Model ownership explicitly and enforce invariants at the database layer.
tasks.solutionCode:
from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models

class Label(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=50, unique=True)

class Ticket(models.Model):
    class Status(models.TextChoices):
        OPEN = "open", "Open"
        CLOSED = "closed", "Closed"
    created_by = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name="created_tickets")
    assignee = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True, related_name="assigned_tickets")
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    description = models.TextField()
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=Status.choices, default=Status.OPEN)
    labels = models.ManyToManyField(Label, blank=True, related_name="tickets")
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

    class Meta:
        constraints = [models.UniqueConstraint(fields=["created_by", "title"], name="unique_ticket_title_per_creator")]
        indexes = [models.Index(fields=["created_by", "-updated_at"]), models.Index(fields=["status", "-updated_at"])]

class Comment(models.Model):
    ticket = models.ForeignKey(Ticket, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="comments")
    author = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name="ticket_comments")
    body = models.TextField()
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The schema makes ownership explicit, preserves historical users/comments with PROTECT, and gives the database responsibility for true uniqueness and common access patterns.

tasks.title: Refactor an N+1 query path
tasks.description: Remove an N+1 relationship access pattern and verify the result with measured query counts.
tasks.problemStatement: A ticket detail view fetches the assignee once and then issues one query per comment author. Refactor the queryset.
objectives: Use select_related for the assignee.
Use prefetch_related for comments and their authors.
Add a query-count assertion around the tested path.
constraints: Do not claim a universal query count without measuring.
Do not prefetch unrelated tables merely for appearance.
tasks.hint: Think first about whether each relationship is single-valued or a collection.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The optimization follows relationship cardinality and should be validated with a test or profiling tool in the actual environment.

modules.assessment: Review schema correctness, migration workflow, and evidence-based optimization.

modules.title: Forms, Authentication, Authorization, and Sessions
modules.description: Build secure browser workflows with server-side validation, Django authentication, object-level authorization, and CSRF protection.
objectives: Validate browser input on the server.
Use Django’s authentication and password-management facilities.
Enforce authorization on objects rather than relying on URL identifiers or UI hiding.
Protect state-changing browser requests with CSRF.

lessons.title: Forms and server-side validation
lessons.description: Build ModelForms and field-level validation.
learningObjectives: Return invalid forms to the user without losing safe input.

notes.text: Client-side validation is useful for usability but cannot be the authoritative security boundary.

quiz.question: Why must the server validate form submissions?
options: Clients can submit crafted requests outside the intended UI
quiz.answer: Clients can submit crafted requests outside the intended UI
quiz.explanation: The server controls the authoritative data boundary, not the browser.

summary: Server-side validation is mandatory for untrusted input.
Forms centralize field and form-level validation.

lessons.title: Authentication, sessions, and password handling
lessons.description: Use Django’s standard user and session facilities instead of inventing password storage.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between authentication and authorization.

notes.text: Authentication associates a request with an identity. Authorization decides what that identity is permitted to access. Django’s built-in framework provides password hashing, sessions, login/logout flows, and permission primitives.
Never log raw passwords or session secrets, and never invent reversible password storage.

quiz.question: What is authentication?
options: Deciding what a user may access
Establishing the identity associated with credentials
quiz.answer: Establishing the identity associated with credentials
quiz.explanation: Authentication establishes who the requester is; authorization determines allowed actions.

summary: Use the framework’s identity machinery.
Treat authorization as a separate decision from authentication.

lessons.title: Object-level authorization
lessons.description: Prevent cross-user access by scoping object retrieval to the authenticated principal.

notes.text: ticket = get_object_or_404(Ticket, pk=ticket_id, created_by=request.user)
A numeric identifier is a reference, not permission. Authorization should be enforced where the object is retrieved or mutated so changing the identifier cannot reveal another user’s record.

quiz.question: Which pattern best prevents IDOR-style ticket access?
options: Scope the object query to the authorized user
quiz.answer: Scope the object query to the authorized user
quiz.explanation: The server-side query boundary prevents unauthorized objects from being returned to the handler.

summary: Authorization belongs in server-side data access decisions.
Do not rely on hidden buttons or disabled client controls.

lessons.title: CSRF, cookies, and secure sessions
lessons.description: Protect state-changing browser requests and understand session cookie attributes.
learningObjectives: Add CSRF tokens to POST forms.
Explain Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite at a practical level.
Align cookie settings with HTTPS deployment.

notes.text:
<form method="post">
  {% csrf_token %}
  <button type="submit">Close ticket</button>
</form>
CSRF is relevant when browsers automatically attach session credentials to requests. Django’s CSRF middleware and token mechanism are designed to protect state-changing browser workflows.
Do not disable CSRF globally just to make a form pass a local test.

quiz.question: What does CSRF protection primarily mitigate?
options: Cross-site forged state-changing requests using a victim’s browser credentials
quiz.answer: Cross-site forged state-changing requests using a victim’s browser credentials
quiz.explanation: CSRF defenses make it harder for another origin to cause authenticated state changes on behalf of a victim.

summary: Cookie-based authentication and CSRF protection must be designed together.
Secure cookies become especially important for HTTPS deployments.

tasks.title: Implement secure ticket creation
tasks.description: Build an authenticated form workflow with server-side validation, CSRF protection, and automatic ownership.
tasks.problemStatement: Authenticated users can create tickets. Ownership must come from request.user, not user-controlled form fields.
objectives: Protect the view with login_required.
Validate input using a ModelForm.
Set created_by from request.user.
Redirect after successful creation.
constraints: Do not expose created_by as a writable field.
Keep the CSRF token in the POST form.
tasks.hint: Trust the authenticated request context for ownership, not hidden inputs.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The view validates untrusted form data, derives ownership from the authenticated principal, and redirects after a successful state change.

modules.assessment: Review security boundaries and confirm authorization decisions cannot be bypassed through crafted requests.

modules.title: JSON APIs and Browser Integration
modules.description: Expose a focused JSON API with Django REST framework and integrate it safely with browser-side fetch.
objectives: Design stable API resources and status-code semantics.
Use DRF serializers, viewsets, permissions, and pagination.
Integrate fetch while understanding same-origin policy and CORS.
Document API behavior for humans and automated clients.

lessons.title: REST resources and status codes
lessons.description: Design a ticket API around predictable resources and response semantics.
learningObjectives: Choose meaningful success and error status codes.
Separate validation errors from server failures.

notes.text: An API is a contract between producer and consumer. A predictable resource model and error shape reduce client-side branching and make automated testing clearer.

items: 201 Created fits successful resource creation.
400 commonly represents invalid client input.
401 and 403 are different concepts and should not be collapsed without reason.

quiz.question: What is a serializer used for in DRF?
quiz.answer: Representing and validating API data
quiz.explanation: DRF serializers convert complex data to representations and validate/deserialise incoming data.

summary: Stable resource naming improves client integration.
HTTP status codes are part of the API contract.

lessons.title: Serializers, viewsets, and permissions
lessons.description: Implement CRUD endpoints while preserving ownership constraints.
learningObjectives: Scope get_queryset to the current user.

notes.text: IsAuthenticated answers who may use the endpoint; it does not by itself answer which object they may access.

quiz.question: Why scope get_queryset to request.user?
options: To limit visible objects to the authorized user
quiz.answer: To limit visible objects to the authorized user
quiz.explanation: The queryset boundary prevents one user from retrieving another user’s objects through normal endpoint operations.

summary: Serializer fields define a data contract.
Queryset scoping creates an object-level authorization boundary.

lessons.title: Fetch, same-origin policy, and CORS
lessons.description: Add a browser-side API call and distinguish CORS from access control.
learningObjectives: Explain why credentialed cross-origin requests need deliberate configuration.

notes.text: CORS is a browser-enforced mechanism that controls whether script-originating cross-origin responses are exposed to web content. It is not an authentication or authorization system.

quiz.question: What does CORS primarily control?
options: Browser exposure of cross-origin responses to scripts
quiz.answer: Browser exposure of cross-origin responses to scripts
quiz.explanation: CORS defines browser rules for cross-origin requests and response exposure.

summary: CORS and authorization solve different problems.
Client code must handle non-success responses deliberately.

lessons.title: Pagination, API errors, and documentation
lessons.description: Make collection endpoints usable as data volume grows.
learningObjectives: Document authentication, writable/read-only fields, and error shapes.
Avoid exposing stack traces in API responses.

items: Bound collection response size with pagination.
Document the request/response contract, including validation errors.
Keep internal exception details in server logs rather than normal responses.

quiz.question: Why paginate an API collection?
options: To bound response size and work per request
quiz.answer: To bound response size and work per request
quiz.explanation: Pagination prevents a growing collection from creating unbounded response payloads and processing.

summary: API consumers need bounded payloads and predictable failures.
Documentation is part of the API interface.

tasks.title: Build an authorized ticket API
tasks.description: Implement a DRF ticket API with serializer validation, ownership scoping, and a regression test for unauthorized access.
tasks.problemStatement: The frontend needs list/create/update capabilities for the current user’s tickets. Another user must not be able to retrieve or mutate those objects.
objectives: Use ModelSerializer with server-controlled fields read-only.
Scope get_queryset to request.user.
Assign ownership during create.
Test a non-owner access attempt.
constraints: Do not invent a custom token scheme.
Do not trust owner identifiers from JSON input.
tasks.hint: Make the authorized data set smaller before any object action is performed.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The serializer validates and protects server-owned fields; the queryset establishes object visibility before DRF retrieves individual records.

modules.assessment: Review API correctness, authorization boundaries, pagination, and client error handling.

modules.title: Testing, Debugging, and Code Review
modules.description: Turn requirements and bug reports into automated evidence using pytest-django and Django testing tools.
objectives: Configure pytest-django for a Django project.
Write model, view, form, and API tests.
Create regression tests from real defects.
Review changes for correctness, security, performance, and maintainability.

lessons.title: Django tests and pytest-django
lessons.description: Build a maintainable test suite with database-aware fixtures.
learningObjectives: Separate unit-like tests from request/integration tests.

notes.text:
[pytest]
DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE = config.settings

import pytest
from django.urls import reverse
from tickets.models import Ticket

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_non_owner_cannot_view_ticket(client, django_user_model):
    owner = django_user_model.objects.create_user(username="owner", password="x")
    other = django_user_model.objects.create_user(username="other", password="y")
    ticket = Ticket.objects.create(created_by=owner, title="Private ticket", description="Details")
    client.force_login(other)
    response = client.get(reverse("ticket-detail", kwargs={"ticket_id": ticket.pk}))
    assert response.status_code == 404

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_owner_can_view_ticket(client, django_user_model):
    owner = django_user_model.objects.create_user(username="owner2", password="x")
    ticket = Ticket.objects.create(created_by=owner, title="Owned ticket", description="Details")
    client.force_login(owner)
    response = client.get(reverse("ticket-detail", kwargs={"ticket_id": ticket.pk}))
    assert response.status_code == 200

project.heading: Build a Production-Oriented Multi-User Issue Tracker with Django and PostgreSQL
project.description: Build a multi-user issue tracker for software teams. Users sign in, create and edit tickets, assign labels and optional assignees, add comments, filter and paginate their tickets, use a JSON API, and close tickets through a transaction-aware domain service. The capstone integrates the major internship competencies: Python application structure, Django, PostgreSQL-oriented persistence, authentication, object-level authorization, forms, CSRF, REST API design, testing, performance reasoning, logging, documentation, and deployment preparation.
project.problemStatement: A small engineering team needs a single source of truth for software issues. The application must make ownership and status visible, preserve comment history, prevent one user from reading another user’s private tickets, support both server-rendered browser workflows and JSON API consumers, and remain understandable and testable as data volume grows.
objectives: Implement the application from written acceptance criteria.
Model and persist the domain with Django ORM and PostgreSQL-oriented configuration.
Implement secure authentication, CSRF protection, validation, and per-object authorization.
Expose a documented JSON API using Django REST framework.
Write automated tests for domain invariants, authorization, views, and API behavior.
Profile query behavior and justify relationship loading and indexes.
Prepare secure environment-driven settings, static-file release steps, logging, health checks, and deployment documentation.
requirements: Environment variables for secrets and deployment-sensitive configuration.
HTTPS for production deployment and a production WSGI/ASGI serving layer.
No real credentials or personal data in source control.
features: Authenticated login/logout using Django’s standard authentication/session facilities.
Ticket CRUD workflows with server-side validation and owner-derived created_by.
Chronological comments associated with protected tickets.
Filtering by status and title search.
JSON list/detail/create/update/close API endpoints protected by authentication and ownership scoping.
Automated regression tests for critical security and domain behavior.

architecture.style: Django modular monolith with server-rendered HTML plus a JSON API.
components: PostgreSQL or SQLite fallback for local development
architecture.dataFlow: User → Browser → Django router → authentication/authorization → form or serializer validation → domain service/ORM → database → template/JSON response → Browser/API client
architecture.errorFlow: User input produces validation errors; unauthorized objects remain outside the authorized queryset; unexpected exceptions are logged internally and returned without sensitive tracebacks.
architecture.deploymentFlow: Git change → automated tests/checks → deployment environment variables → database migration → static-file collection → production WSGI/ASGI server → HTTPS and operational monitoring

fileWiseSolution.code:
from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models

class Label(models.Model):
    name=models.CharField(max_length=50,unique=True)
    class Meta: ordering=["name"]
    def __str__(self): return self.name

class Ticket(models.Model):
    class Status(models.TextChoices):
        OPEN="open","Open"
        CLOSED="closed","Closed"
    created_by=models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,on_delete=models.PROTECT,related_name="created_tickets")
    assignee=models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,on_delete=models.SET_NULL,null=True,blank=True,related_name="assigned_tickets")
    title=models.CharField(max_length=200)
    description=models.TextField()
    status=models.CharField(max_length=20,choices=Status.choices,default=Status.OPEN)
    labels=models.ManyToManyField(Label,blank=True,related_name="tickets")
    created_at=models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated_at=models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)
    class Meta:
        constraints=[models.UniqueConstraint(fields=["created_by","title"],name="unique_ticket_title_per_creator")]
        indexes=[models.Index(fields=["created_by","-updated_at"]),models.Index(fields=["status","-updated_at"])]
        ordering=["-updated_at","-id"]
    def __str__(self): return self.title

class Comment(models.Model):
    ticket=models.ForeignKey(Ticket,on_delete=models.CASCADE,related_name="comments")
    author=models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,on_delete=models.PROTECT,related_name="ticket_comments")
    body=models.TextField()
    created_at=models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    class Meta: ordering=["created_at","id"]

fileWiseSolution.code:
# Issue Tracker

A multi-user Django issue tracker used as the Python Web Development Internship capstone.

## Local setup
1. Create and activate `.venv`.
2. Install project and test dependencies.
3. Supply a development `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` and database configuration.
4. Run `python manage.py migrate`.
5. Run `pytest`.
6. Use `python manage.py runserver` only for development.

## Production preparation
Run migrations, collect static files, and `python manage.py check --deploy`. Use a production WSGI/ASGI server and HTTPS. Keep real secrets outside Git.

project.howItWorks: The request enters Django through the URL dispatcher. Authentication middleware associates the request with a user. HTML views and API viewsets retrieve only objects owned by that user, so an identifier alone cannot grant access. Browser forms pass through Django validation and CSRF protection; API payloads pass through DRF serializer validation. Domain operations such as closing a ticket can use transaction.atomic so the ticket state and an optional audit comment succeed or roll back together. The ORM persists state to PostgreSQL in production-oriented configuration. Tests exercise the model, HTTP, and API boundaries. During release, migrations and static collection are run before the application is served through a production WSGI/ASGI server behind HTTPS.
project.dataFlow: User → Browser/API client → Django URL router → authentication → ownership authorization → Form/Serializer validation → service/ORM → PostgreSQL → response/redirect/JSON → client
project.testing: Run `pytest`. Critical tests should cover creation ownership, uniqueness constraints, authentication-required views, non-owner denial, API validation, and API visibility. Use query-count assertions or profiling tools when optimizing. Only report tests as passing when they have actually been run in the relevant environment.
securityReview: Keep real secrets and DATABASE_URL credentials outside Git.
Use Django’s standard password hashing and session authentication.
Keep CSRF protection enabled for cookie-authenticated browser POST actions.
Scope object retrieval by authenticated user ownership.
Keep server-controlled fields read-only in serializers.
Rely on template autoescaping for normal user content.
Do not log passwords, tokens, or unnecessary sensitive values.
Use HTTPS and secure cookies in production.
Run `check --deploy` and perform an independent security review.
performanceReview: Measure representative query counts before and after relationship loading changes.
Use select_related for suitable single-valued relationships.
Use prefetch_related for suitable related collections.
Use pagination to bound collection size.
Add indexes based on observed filters/orderings and inspect query plans.
Do not fabricate performance benchmarks; capture them only from real measurement.
troubleshooting: For import failures, verify interpreter identity and package installation before changing application code.
For template errors, inspect template paths, DIRS, APP_DIRS, and template names.
For static-file issues, verify STATIC_URL, static tags, collectstatic, and deployment static serving.
For CSRF 403 responses, inspect token placement, cookie settings, and trusted-origin configuration before disabling protection.
For cross-user object access, reproduce with two test users and add a regression test.
For database mismatch, inspect migrations, applied migration state, and the configured database URL.
